{"id": "20:56/q06", "question": "What is the force of 'all' in 'all Our signs'?", "turns_on": "The relevant domain of 'all': each familiar sign, all categories or details, or an idiom for abundance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q06/p1", "position": "It includes every sign in the relevant known set, without claiming every sign God has.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya restricts 'all' to signs shown to Pharaoh; Tabrisi and Ibn al-Jawzi exclude all God's signs. Samin says the emphatic word rules out a mere subset and fits inward perception of proofs of oneness and prophecy. Baydawi says it can cover every individual. Bursevi says it confirms the familiar kinds. Ibn Ashur says this totality intensifies wonder and compares 54:41–42."}, {"id": "20:56/q06/p2", "position": "It confirms every kind or category of sign.", "reasons": "Baydawi offers categories as well as individuals; Bursevi says every kind was included. Alusi reports an all-kinds proposal but objects that its proposed categories may not exhaust miracles."}, {"id": "20:56/q06/p3", "position": "It emphasizes every implication and detail of the displayed signs, leaving Pharaoh no excuse.", "reasons": "Alusi says many particulars are not enumerated yet every implication and detail was before Pharaoh; his account also allows plural wording for the many details within the staff and hand."}, {"id": "20:56/q06/p4", "position": "Arabic idiom permits 'all' here to mean many or very many signs.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu explicitly prefers this reading over taking the phrase as literally every sign."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q07", "question": "When were the signs shown and the denial described?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse summarizes the whole confrontation or is read in strict sequence before the magicians' summons.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q07/p1", "position": "The verse surveys signs shown across Moses' mission and Pharaoh's continuing pattern of denial.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the staff, hand and other signs came over time; Tabatabai includes those before Pharaoh's drowning and says denial was a general pattern, not only the first encounter. Ibn Ashur says Pharaoh denied even after the signs and entered the parted sea seeking the Israelites; he rejects taking the verse as proof that all signs preceded the summoning of magicians, since many came later and waw need not imply sequence. Alusi says many of the nine signs appeared much later."}, {"id": "20:56/q07/p2", "position": "The focus is the initial staff and hand shown in response to Pharaoh's demand.", "reasons": "Alusi cites 7:106–108 and argues that the later emergence of most of the nine signs makes their inclusion at this point strained. Abu Hayyan and Samin report the argument that only the staff and hand had yet been seen."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q08", "question": "What does the 'fa' before 'he denied' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q08/p1", "position": "Pharaoh denied immediately after the showing, without hesitation.", "reasons": "Alusi says the fa marks immediate sequence; Bursevi likewise stresses denial without pause."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q09", "question": "What did Pharaoh deny?", "turns_on": "Whether the unstated object is the signs and their divine origin, Moses and his message, a report, or the proof.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q09/p1", "position": "He denied the signs and their truth, branding them magic.", "reasons": "Muqatil says he rejected their divine origin and claimed magic. Yahya, Nahhas, Wahidi-Wajiz, Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Nasafi, Tabrisi, Biqai, Bursevi and Study Quran describe denial of the signs. Wahidi-Basit says he treated them as lies or accused Moses of lying. Abu Hayyan reports denial of divine origin and the magic charge; Alusi says the omitted object can be the signs. Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir relate denial to firsthand sight and cite 27:14 for knowingly unjust rejection."}, {"id": "20:56/q09/p2", "position": "He called Moses a liar and denied his message.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Basit gives this as an alternative to treating the signs as lies. Jishumi says Pharaoh called Moses a liar, refused the call to worship God, then accused him of sorcery to mislead his people. Abu Hayyan says the unspoken object may be Moses and his message; Baydawi describes denial of Moses."}, {"id": "20:56/q09/p3", "position": "He denied the report brought to him.", "reasons": "Mawardi offers this wording together with refusal of obedience."}, {"id": "20:56/q09/p4", "position": "He rejected the proof presented to him.", "reasons": "Mawardi offers this as an alternative to denial of a report; Tabrisi also gives rejected proof as an alternative formulation."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q10", "question": "Why did Pharaoh deny despite the signs?", "turns_on": "Whether rejection is described as knowingly arrogant or, in the inward reading, as incapacity rooted in attachment to matter.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q10/p1", "position": "He knowingly rejected them through arrogance, obstinacy and transgression.", "reasons": "Tabari, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi and Alusi stress deliberate persistence; Qurtubi says direct sight sharpened the obstinacy and compares those who inwardly knew but rejected unjustly in 27:14. Abu Hayyan rejects confusion because 27:14 says Pharaoh knew the signs. Ibn Kathir cites the same verse. Wahidi-Basit says Pharaoh called Moses a magician; Alusi says even a cognitive reading of arayna must retain knowing denial. Ibn Ashur emphasizes his persistence despite many signs."}, {"id": "20:56/q10/p2", "position": "His attachment to matter prevented him from perceiving immaterial truth and made him call the proof magic.", "reasons": "Qashani's inward explanation says Pharaoh resisted departure from his bodily dwelling."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q11", "question": "Why is the object of 'denied' left unspoken?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q11/p1", "position": "The omission magnifies what he denied while leaving the object understood.", "reasons": "Samin gives this rhetorical explanation. Abu Hayyan and Alusi name the signs as the apparent object and Moses or his message as a possible object."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q12", "question": "What does 'abā' mean here and what did Pharaoh refuse?", "turns_on": "The unstated object of refusal: faith and acceptance generally, worship and obedience specifically, or release of the Israelites.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q12/p1", "position": "He refused faith, submission, obedience and acceptance of the truth or signs.", "reasons": "Jishumi glosses iba as refusing or refraining; Bursevi calls it intense refusal, stronger than ordinary refusal. Yahya, Nahhas, Wahidi-Wajiz, Baghawi, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Baydawi, Alusi and Study Quran specify belief, acceptance, submission or obedience. Mawardi pairs refusal of obedience with denial of a report and refusal of proof with rejecting it. Muqatil says Pharaoh denied divine origin and refused belief."}, {"id": "20:56/q12/p2", "position": "He refused the call to worship and obey God.", "reasons": "Jishumi explicitly identifies the call, after Pharaoh branded Moses a liar; Wahidi-Basit specifies monotheism."}, {"id": "20:56/q12/p3", "position": "He refused to send the Israelites.", "reasons": "Biqai gives this as the concrete refusal in the Moses–Pharaoh confrontation."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q13", "question": "What does Pharaoh's refusal imply about responsibility for his actions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q13/p1", "position": "His refusal was his own acquired act, making reward and punishment applicable.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says wa-aba establishes deliberate acquisition; Abu Hayyan reports Ibn Atiyya and Abi giving acquisition as the basis of recompense."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q14", "question": "What did the serpent sign reportedly look like and cause?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in the serpent's size, actions and the consequences for the crowd.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q14/p1", "position": "It was an eighty-cubit terrifying serpent; Pharaoh fled, a crowd crush killed twenty-five thousand, and he begged Moses to remove it.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this from Wahb ibn Munabbih; Moses removed it and it became a staff again."}, {"id": "20:56/q14/p2", "position": "It rose a mile, swooped at Pharaoh, spoke to Moses, and returned to a staff after Pharaoh pleaded.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this separate account, with a different scale and sequence."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q15", "question": "How was the hand sign reportedly seen?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q15/p1", "position": "Moses' hand shone with luminous whiteness brighter than the sun, attracting onlookers' wonder.", "reasons": "Alusi gives this report of the hand."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q16", "question": "How does this sentence fit the surrounding Moses–Pharaoh narrative?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is a retrospective summary or a strict chronological explanation of Pharaoh's earlier question.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q16/p1", "position": "It resumes and summarizes the confrontation before the ensuing dialogue.", "reasons": "Alusi calls it a brief recap. Ibn Ashur says it introduces the dialogue, may coordinate with 20:49 after ellipsis or stand parenthetically, and generalizes the signs here unlike al-Araf's successive enumeration in 7:133. Biqai says this concise account is more forceful than al-Araf's fuller list. Tabatabai treats denial as the whole pattern. Ibn Ashur objects to commentators who join it to 20:49 as an explanation requiring all signs before the magicians; waw need not impose sequence."}, {"id": "20:56/q16/p2", "position": "It explains Pharaoh's challenge in 20:49 as his response after the signs.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports this common coordination by commentators but objects that many signs came much later and waw does not require chronological sequence."}]}

{"id": "20:56/q18", "question": "What setting and purpose explain the coming contest with magicians?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q18/p1", "position": "Egyptian political anxiety and magic's public religious influence shaped the contest, which gave Pharaoh and his elite another test.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says Israelite presence and Moses' wish to take them home alarmed Pharaoh's government; magic strongly influenced the people, so Pharaoh's elite used and rewarded magicians as a weapon against monotheism. {"id": "20:56/q19", "question": "What other accounts are readers directed to compare with this episode?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q19/p1", "position": "The Qur'anic account in 7:103–126 and the Biblical account.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu explicitly directs comparison with both accounts; Islahi says details of the signs are given in the Torah."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q20", "question": "What does a cited poetic example show about deliberate grammatical relations?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q20/p1", "position": "A poet intentionally orders words by their grammatical relations rather than uttering them without syntactic awareness.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani says Imru al-Qays knew nabki answers the imperative qifa, dhikra is annexed to habib, and manzil is coordinated with it."}]}
{"id": "20:56/q21", "question": "How is 'kullahā' parsed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q21/p1", "position": "It is accusative as an adjective qualifying āyāt.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives this iʿrāb."}]}
{"id": "20:69/q01", "question": "What does the command to cast mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q01/p1", "position": "Throw or cast the object away.", "reasons": "Jishumi equates ilqāʾ with ṭarḥ, nabdh, and ramy."}]}
{"id": "20:69/q02", "question": "Who is addressed by the command?", "turns_on": "The implicit addressee may be Moses or the staff.", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q02/p1", "position": "Moses is addressed.", "reasons": "Qurtubi gives Moses as one possible addressee; Ibn Kathir says God inspired him to cast the staff."}, {"id": "20:69/q02/p2", "position": "The staff may be addressed.", "reasons": "Qurtubi gives this as another grammatical possibility."}]}

{"id": "20:69/q04", "question": "Why call the staff 'what is in your right hand'?", "turns_on": "The explanations turn on small appearance, extraordinary power, right-hand connotations, and prior mention.", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q04/p1", "position": "The indirect wording magnifies its extraordinary power.", "reasons": "Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi contrast it with the many implements. Alusi objects that this ignores the staff's prior extraordinary state."}, {"id": "20:69/q04/p3", "position": "It recalls God's earlier question and encourages Moses.", "reasons": "Biqai and Alusi cite 20:17; Alusi says this wording suits removal of fear, while 7:117 gives the command by meaning. {"id": "20:69/q05", "question": "Where did Moses' staff come from?", "turns_on": "Mawardi transmits differing origin reports.", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q05/p1", "position": "An ʿawsaj thorn tree.", "reasons": "Mawardi reports Wahb."}, {"id": "20:69/q05/p2", "position": "Paradise.", "reasons": "Mawardi reports Ibn Abbas, who says Moses killed ʿUj ibn ʿAnaq with it."}]}
{"id": "20:69/q06", "question": "What does تَلْقَفْ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q06/p1", "position": "To seize swiftly or swallow, here by mouth.", "reasons": "Hasan specifies its mouth. Jishumi compares laqifa, talaqqafa and iltaqafa; Kisa'i says taking quickly. Qurtubi cites laqif thaqif for a deft person and also wall or basin collapse; Bursevi cites taking by hand or mouth. {"id": "20:69/q07", "question": "How is تَلْقَفْ read and construed?", "turns_on": "The ending marks command consequence versus circumstance or assertion, while the consonants reflect different forms and routes.", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q07/p1", "position": "Indicative with raised fāʾ and doubled qāf, as circumstance or new clause.", "reasons": "Ibn Amir, especially Ibn Dhakwan, is named. Zajjaj allows the syntax but says it was not established for his recitation. Al-Farisi allows Moses or staff as subject, using 8:17 and 5:95; Tabrisi cites 99:4. Qiraat-ER emphasizes independent assertion. Ibn Mujahid names Ibn Amir alone for the raised fāʾ and doubled qāf. Ibn Khalawayh derives the doubled form from tatalaqqafu with one tāʾ omitted; he allows an understood fāʾ ('and it will gulp') or a circumstantial clause describing mā, citing 94:6."}, {"id": "20:69/q07/p2", "position": "Jussive with doubled qāf, answering the command.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and others supply an implied condition: if cast, it swallows. Ibn Mujahid says the readers other than Ibn Amir, including Abu Bakr from Asim, have the jussive. Ibn Khalawayh explains the doubled jussive as the consequence of the imperative."}, {"id": "20:69/q07/p3", "position": "Jussive with light qāf and still lām, from laqifa.", "reasons": "Hafs is widely named; Qurtubi also names Sulami, Abu Hayyan adds Abu Jafar and Isma, and Ibn Mujahid and Farisi report Qunbul or al-Nabbal. Nasafi also names Ibn Dhakwan. Ibn Mujahid specifies that Hafs from Asim has still lām, light qāf and jussive fāʾ. Ibn Khalawayh derives the light form from laqifa yalqafu and treats it as the consequence of the imperative."}, {"id": "20:69/q07/p4", "position": "Doubled initial tāʾ from tatalaqqaf.", "reasons": "Al-Bazzi and Ibn Fulayh transmit it from Ibn Kathir, in connected recitation. Ibn Atiyya notes no initial alif is then needed. Al-Farisi objects that hamzat al-wasl cannot enter imperfect verbs; Ahmad ibn Musa starts lightly. Tabrisi gives the same difficulty; NASHR lists 31 such verbs. Ibn Khalawayh reports Ibn Kathir's doubling of the initial tāʾ here and in more than thirty similar forms."}, {"id": "20:69/q07/p5", "position": "Talqamu, with mīm, is transmitted.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi names Ibn Masud, Ubayy, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Raja, referring to 7:117; Qurtubi lists synonymous talaqqama."}]}

{"id": "20:69/q17", "question": "How is كَيْدُ سَٰحِرٍ read and understood?", "turns_on": "The variants differ in agent versus craft and nominative predicate versus accusative object.", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q17/p1", "position": "Kaydu siḥr: nominative 'a plot of magic'.", "reasons": "Hamza, al-Kisai and Khalaf are named, with Kufans except Asim. Zajjaj supplies the syntax."}]}
